name: Beth Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior songwriter on a small deal with Harbour Lane, a music publisher with about twenty writers. They pay me a small monthly advance, which is money up front against future royalties, and in return I write toplines, the melody and words that go over someone else's track. Most days I'm in a tiny writing room with a producer, trying to land a chorus in four hours. I also sing the demos, and on Wednesdays I play my own songs at an open mic in a café on Canal Street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit into your day already?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All over it, honestly. I use it for rhyme ideas, to mock up a backing track at two in the morning, to check if a melody sounds too much like an existing hit. It makes me faster, and I'm not the most gifted writer in the building, so speed matters. I live alone in a studio flat, and I've got about four months of costs saved. The Harbour Lane deal comes up for renewal next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a handy assistant and that's all. I'd probably post a reel of how I use it to write, because people find that interesting. I'd say the real skill is still knowing what a good chorus feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problem is the renewal, not AI. I've had two cuts on released songs in eighteen months, which is not great. If Harbour Lane doesn't renew me, I'm back to bar work and open mics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write as much as I can before the summer and push for more sessions with the better producers. I'd use the tools to turn ideas around faster. I'd keep my savings and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but focused. It's the normal pressure of being a junior writer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a 'cut' mean, for someone outside the industry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cut is when an artist actually records and releases your song. That's when royalties start. Two cuts in eighteen months is the number that decides whether a music publisher keeps paying a junior writer like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the renewal fell through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bar work at night, keep writing in the day, and pitch songs to independent artists directly. I'd survive, I've done it before. It just means a year of being tired.

I'd say the real skill is knowing what a **good chorus** feels like.
think: My real problem is the **deal renewal** next summer, not AI.
**Two cuts** in eighteen months isn't great for a junior writer.
do: Write as much as possible and push for sessions with **better producers**.
Use AI tools to **turn ideas** around faster.
feel: **Tense** but **focused**, the normal pressure of a junior writer.
S0.quote: Two cuts in eighteen months is the number that decides whether a music publisher keeps paying a junior writer like me.
fieldNote: Her main worry is **contract renewal**, which exists with or without AI.

Her fallback is **bar work**, which she's done before.

steps.text: Book extra writing sessions with Harbour Lane's top producers
Use AI backing tracks to finish song demos the same day
Pitch songs directly to independent artists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say writers who use AI well will do fine and the ones who refuse won't. I'd also say publishers need clear rules on who owns a song made with AI. I'd be practical, not doom and gloom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think topline writing gets crowded fast. If a label can get a hundred AI choruses overnight, they'll only pay for the very best human ones, and I'm not the very best. Harbour Lane would drop the juniors first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift towards being an artist, building my own audience online, because people follow a person, not a song file. I'd offer my AI skills to Harbour Lane, running the tools for the senior writers. I'd also start doing short-form music for brands' social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a bit buzzed too. It's scary and it's also the kind of change I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Harbour Lane actually pay you to run the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, for a while. Somebody has to know which buttons to press and which output is rubbish. I'd rather be the songwriter who runs the AI for Harbour Lane (her music publisher) than the songwriter the AI replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is building an audience realistic at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a long shot. But I've got four hundred people who come to the Wednesday café nights over a year, which is a start. I'd film every night and post it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a pause on the hype and a plan for people, quickly, because two years is too fast. I'd say it in writers' groups and on my channels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, songwriting as a paid job for someone like me is over by 2028. It's all thinking work, no hands-on part. The only bit with any time is singing live, which robots don't touch until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop writing for the publisher and go all in on live performing for a year or two. I'd play every café, wedding and bar that would pay, and build a following. I'd cut my spending hard and maybe move back to my mum's place to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one about tech, but two years doesn't leave room to be clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I need her spare room for a year and I'll pay her in groceries. My mum always said music was a hobby, and asking for my old room back would feel like proving my mum right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money run out first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, obviously. Four months goes fast without the advance. Then I'd sell my good microphone, which would hurt.

I'd say it in **writers' groups** and on my channels.
think: Paid **songwriting** for someone like me is over by 2028.
Only **singing live** has time, until robots arrive in 2031.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose her deal** and all writing income quickly.
She separates **thinking work** from **live singing**, which buys time.

steps.text: Book paid sets at cafés, bars and weddings every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to adapt if people start now. I'd post about how writers can move into live work and teaching. I'd also want some kind of fair copyright deal for human writers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get two more years at Harbour Lane, maybe three if I'm useful with the tools. Then writing jobs dry up. Live performing has until 2034, which is real time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the AI tools for the publisher while that lasts and save hard. I'd build my live act on the side: café nights, weddings, a small tour. I might take a vocal coaching course so I can teach singing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel in charge of it. Five years is enough to set up the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching singing, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a voice is a body thing. You need someone in the room watching your breath and your shoulders. A computer can write a better chorus than me, but a computer can't stand beside a nervous teenager and fix the teenager's breathing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you save, realistically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I kept the advance and played gigs, maybe two hundred a month. In three years that's a decent cushion for the switch.

I'd want a fair **copyright deal** for human writers.
think: I'd get **two or three years** at Harbour Lane, then writing dries up.
**Live performing** has until 2034, which is real time.
do: Run **AI tools** for the publisher while it lasts.

S3.quote: A computer can write a better chorus than me, but a computer can't stand beside a nervous teenager and fix the teenager's breathing.
fieldNote: She sees **teaching singing** as hands-on work a machine can't do.

steps.text: Run AI writing tools for Harbour Lane while the deal lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's make sure training and copyright rules are sorted early. I'd post about it but not obsess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade means I can have a proper go at being an artist and build teaching on the side. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI lands, forty for robots. That's enough to build something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Harbour Lane, use the tools to write more and better, and push for my own cuts. I'd start teaching a few singing pupils within two years. I'd put a bit into a pension, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, mostly fine. It feels like the future I'd have had anyway, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pension is a big step. What made you say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years I can actually picture being forty. Ten years of warning is the first time I've pictured myself at forty as a singer instead of a girl with a laptop and a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the music still doesn't work out by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be a singing teacher with a following and some savings. A singing teacher with forty loyal pupils is a better job than most junior songwriters ever get.

I'd post about it but **not obsess**.
think: A decade lets me have a proper go as an **artist**.
I'd be **thirty-seven** when thinking AI lands, forty for robots.
do: Stay at Harbour Lane and push for my own **cuts**.
Start teaching a few **singing pupils** within two years.
S4.quote: A singing teacher with forty loyal pupils is a better job than most junior songwriters ever get.
fieldNote: The decade makes her picture **being forty**, which she hadn't before.
A **pension** appearing here signals real long-term planning.
Her fallback of **teaching singing** sounds like a career, not a defeat.

steps.text: Use AI tools to write more songs and chase cuts
Start teaching singing to five pupils within two years
Open a pension and pay in monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because writing is all thinking work and I'd lose it before I'd built a live act or a teaching base. What would help is a fair copyright deal so human writers get paid when their songs train these systems, and maybe short courses in teaching that don't cost a fortune.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the songs would still be any good. I think AI songs will be very good. I just think people will still want to know there's a person who meant it.

headlineQuote: Ten years of warning is the first time I've pictured myself at forty as a singer instead of a girl with a laptop and a deadline.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old junior songwriter** on a small publishing deal who sings demos and open mics.
She uses **AI daily** to write faster, lives alone and has about four months saved.
She's **centre-ground and adaptive**, focused on copyright rules rather than blame.
She expects **topline writing** to go fast and moves towards live singing and teaching.
A longer timeline lets her picture a **pension** and a career as a performer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because writing is all thinking work and goes **first**.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair copyright deal** so human writers get paid for training data.
